title: Beyond Autoregression: Discrete Diffusion for Complex Reasoning and Planning

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to explain why autoregressive (AR) models fail on complex reasoning/planning tasks and why diffusion models are superior. Paper [7] ("ALPINE") investigates planning capabilities in autoregressive language models, modeling planning as a network path-finding task and analyzing limitations of AR models in long-horizon tasks. Paper [10] ("Reasoning with Language Model is Planning with World Model") discusses LLM reasoning failures in planning tasks due to the absence of an internal world model, which aligns with the broader purpose of explaining AR model failures in planning. Paper [16] ("LLM+P") also addresses AR model limitations in long-horizon planning tasks and contrasts them with classical planners. These papers share the same problem-class level objective of understanding AR model failures in planning tasks and exploring alternatives.

### Mechanism
The contribution introduces and analyzes "subgoal imbalance" as a perspective, providing theoretical and empirical evidence that diffusion models decompose difficult subgoals into multiple easier-to-learn views under a multi-view learning framework. Paper [5] ("Unsupervised Multi-view Learning") discusses multi-view learning frameworks and their ability to integrate information from different views to enhance learning, which aligns with the multi-view decomposition mechanism. Paper [26] ("Multi-View Latent Diffusion") employs a score-based diffusion model to impute missing views, demonstrating the use of multi-view frameworks in diffusion models. Paper [18] ("Gradient Guidance for Diffusion Models") establishes a mathematical framework for guided diffusion models, linking diffusion training objectives to optimization theory, which overlaps with the theoretical analysis of diffusion models in the contribution. These papers collectively cover the mechanism at the primitive level.

### Evaluation
The contribution evaluates AR and reverse AR models on synthetic planning tasks, showing their performance degrades at planning distances (PD) ≥ 2, while diffusion models achieve perfect accuracy across all PDs. Paper [7] ("ALPINE") uses synthetic planning tasks to evaluate AR models' planning capabilities, employing a similar benchmark family and validation setup. Paper [16] ("LLM+P") evaluates AR models and classical planners on long-horizon planning tasks, using synthetic benchmarks to validate planning proficiency. Paper [23] ("Resisting Stochastic Risks in Diffusion Planners") evaluates diffusion planners on long-horizon tasks, addressing stochastic risks and reliability. These papers reuse the same evaluation design (synthetic planning benchmarks and metrics), even if applied to different models or tasks.

### Domain
The contribution operates in the domain of language model reasoning and planning. Paper [7] ("ALPINE") explicitly addresses planning capabilities in autoregressive language models. Paper [10] ("Reasoning with Language Model is Planning with World Model") focuses on reasoning and planning tasks in LLMs. Paper [16] ("LLM+P") explores planning proficiency in LLMs and classical planners. All these papers work within the same general application area of language model reasoning and planning, even if targeting different sub-problems or datasets.

### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to improve the learning effectiveness and convergence speed of discrete diffusion models in complex planning tasks. Paper [2] introduces a multi-granularity diffusion model for time series forecasting, aiming to address instability and enhance modeling effectiveness, but it does not target discrete diffusion models or complex planning tasks. Paper [16] focuses on speeding up diffusion model training by optimizing time steps but does not address learning effectiveness in complex planning tasks. No prior paper explicitly shares the same objective of improving discrete diffusion models for complex planning tasks.

### Mechanism
The contribution proposes Multi-Granularity Diffusion Modeling (MGDM), which adds token-level reweighting to sequence-level reweighting, prioritizing learning based on subgoal difficulty. Paper [3] introduces difficulty-weighted learning, dynamically deciding example difficulty during training, which aligns conceptually with token-level reweighting based on difficulty. Paper [24] proposes dynamic data selection for curriculum learning via ability estimation, which also involves prioritizing training examples based on difficulty. Paper [7] discusses reweighting augmented samples, and Paper [15] introduces neural conditional reweighting, both of which involve reweighting mechanisms but do not explicitly combine token-level and sequence-level reweighting. Paper [9] discusses semantic token reweighting for text embeddings, which is token-level reweighting but does not involve sequence-level reweighting or subgoal difficulty prioritization. Paper [3] is the closest match, as it introduces a difficulty-weighted learning mechanism conceptually equivalent to prioritizing subgoal difficulty.

### Evaluation
The contribution evaluates its method through ablation studies (Table 3), comparing token-level and sequence-level reweighting, easy-first decoding, and multi-granularity loss convergence. Paper [3] conducts ablation studies to validate difficulty-weighted learning, which matches the evaluation design of comparing reweighting mechanisms. Paper [24] uses dynamic data selection and probes model ability, which involves evaluating curriculum learning strategies but does not directly match the ablation design for token-level and sequence-level reweighting. Paper [7] evaluates reweighting augmented samples, which aligns with the evaluation design of comparing reweighting mechanisms. Paper [10] evaluates easy-first decoding strategies, which matches the evaluation design for decoding methods. Paper [16] evaluates convergence speed improvements in diffusion models, which aligns with the evaluation design for multi-granularity loss convergence. The evaluation design is covered by multiple prior papers.

### Domain
The contribution operates in the domain of language model inference and planning. Paper [6] applies diffusion models to sequence generative modeling, which overlaps with language model inference. Paper [22] applies diffusion models to textual data generation, which also overlaps with language model inference. Paper [18] applies curriculum learning to job shop scheduling, which overlaps with planning tasks. Paper [19] addresses continual language learning, which overlaps with language model inference. The domain is covered by multiple prior papers.
